newsitem.title: UK: UK audit bureau seeks to measure Internet usage.
newsitem.headline: UK audit bureau seeks to measure Internet usage.

text.p: Britain's Audit Bureau of Circulation expects to soon offer audit services for electronic publishers on the Internet's World Wide Web, paving the way for publishers to set advertising rate cards, an executive with the audit bureau said on Friday.

"The issue is whether or not an independently commissioned currency that everyone believes in will make a difference in advertising revenue to the Internet," Richard Foan, head of the audit bureau's electronic media division, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
At the end of November the bureau will complete a three-month audit test for three Web site publishers. The results are expected to form the basis of an audit system for Web site visits, Foan said.
The three audit test sites include the Electronic Telegraph, Channel 4 and News International.

The bureau initiated the audit tests last summer after receiving requests from more than 100 Web site operators for an audit system. The Electronic Telegraph, an on-line version of Hollinger Inc's Telegraph newspaper, was the first to request an audit service about one year ago, Foan said. Channel 4, one of two terrestrial, commercial television stations in Britain, and News International, a unit of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp and publisher of papers including the Times and the Sun, were among others who also saw the need.
"We're hoping to draw up a rate card and charge for advertising," Sophie Walpole, editor for the Channel 4 Web site, told Reuters.
Channel 4, which launched its Web site last summer, was intent from the outset on measuring Web site visits in a meaningful way so it could charge for advertising.

"Everybody bandies hits and visitors, but what does it mean," Walpole said. "Does it mean one person visited your site 10 times or you've had visits by 10 people? We need to know the number of individuals."
There are Web site audit services currently being offered by several companies, but Foan said that unlike the audit bureau they are not independent, not-for-profit groups.

The audit bureau's efforts are part of a wider effort by the International Federation of Audit Bureaux to develop a single standard for auditing Web site visits. The federation is to meet on December 12 in Frankfurt to try and hammer out audit standards.

In the meantime, Britain's audit bureau is measuring Web site visits by tracking the electronic addresses of all users, as well as the date and time of their visits to each page on the Web. Web sites that ask users to register provide fuller demographic information.
Although similar to the auditing of print publications, Foan said the Web offers far greater information on what users are reading and when -- which could make it highly valuable to advertisers.
By knowing when a Web page is getting its peak use, an advertiser could select at what times of day to place a banner ad on that site, Foan said.
Print publishers, by contrast, can only measure the number of copies sold, without knowing which pages readers are actually turning to.
